newsitem.title: INDIA: Award-winning India writer says crusade not over.
newsitem.headline: Award-winning India writer says crusade not over.

text.p: The Indian novelist who won the Ramon Magsaysay award on Thursday for her crusade to help tribal peoples said she still had a long way to go in her mission.

"I will continue to do the work for the tribals, non-tribal poor and people in distress and write for them," Mahasweta Devi said after the Magsaysay Foundation named her for the 1997 award for journalism, literature and creative communication arts.

"It is good to win awards, but my life is becoming more and more crowded. I am getting little time to concentrate on my writing," the 71-year-old writer in the Bengali language told Reuters in her eastern Indian city of Calcutta.
Devi said tribals inspired her work that brought her the award, which includes $50,000 in cash. "I know they will be very happy," she said.

Devi started her career in 1956 and in 1973 published her watershed novel "Hajar Chaurashir Maa" (Mother of 1084), which is about a grieving mother coming to terms with her murdered son who had joined a Maoist tribal uprising in the 1960s.
"I think it's an eminently deserved award," said movie-maker Govind Nihalani, who is currently filming the celebrated novel.
"For her the next step should be a Nobel Prize," Nihalani said. "I have been familiar with her literature for a long time. It is committed literature and that is one of its strengths."

Born on January 14, 1926, in Dhaka, now the capital of Bangladesh, Devi had her early education in Santiniketan, a rural centre of liberal learning run by Rabindaranath Tagore, India's only Nobel literature laureate.
She majored in English literature at Calcutta University.

During the 1970s, Devi travelled through the countryside of her home state of West Bengal and wrote a series of articles in a Bengali-language newspaper campaigning against police, landlords, politicians and officials who abused tribal people.
"She is not only a writer, but also a social activist. She has done a very remarkable job for the tribals," said Sunil Gangopadhyay, a leading Bengali novelist and poet.
"I haven't seen such a spirited lady," he said.

In 1966, Devi published her first historical biography "Queen of Jhansi," on the life of Laxmibai, who in 1857 battled India's British colonial rulers during an abortive mutiny that later came to be called India's first war of independence.
"Devi's searing stories and novels not only give voice to India's forgotten tribals, but also stress the profound subordination of women in Indian society," the Magsaysay citation said.
